content.stem: A higher echo amplitude from an indication means the reflector is:
options: Not necessarily larger, since amplitude also depends on orientation and type
Always larger than a lower-amplitude one here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain always a whole crack here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Just plain always rejectable here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Amplitude depends on reflector size, orientation, shape, and type together, so a stronger echo does not by itself mean a larger or more severe flaw. Sizing and evaluation use defined techniques, not amplitude alone.
distractors: A favorably oriented small reflector can out-amplitude a larger poorly oriented one.
Amplitude does not identify the flaw type by itself.
Acceptance depends on the criteria applied, not amplitude alone.

content.stem: A planar flaw such as lack of sidewall fusion gives the strongest response when the beam strikes it:
options: Close to perpendicular to the flaw face
At a whole grazing angle here, oddly
Just plain parallel to the whole flaw here
From directly above only here, oddly
content.explanation: Planar reflectors are specular, so the echo back to the probe is strongest when the beam hits the face near normal incidence. Poor angle choice can under-respond a real planar flaw.
distractors: A grazing angle reflects energy away from the probe, lowering the response.
A beam parallel to the flaw face barely intercepts it.
Sidewall fusion faces are angled along the bevel, not addressed only from above.

content.stem: Beam spread tends to make a small reflector's apparent length in the data:
options: Larger than its true length
Smaller than its true length
Exactly its true length
Zero
content.explanation: A diverging beam keeps the reflector in the sound field over extra probe travel, so amplitude-based length can overstate true length. Sizing technique and beam width are accounted for to limit this.
distractors: Spread broadens, not narrows, the apparent extent.
Beam width adds to the measured extent, so it is not exact.
A detected reflector has a non-zero apparent length.

content.stem: Focusing the beam at the depth of interest improves sizing mainly by:
options: Narrowing the beam, improving lateral resolution there
Just raising the whole material velocity here, somehow oddly
Removing all the artifacts here, somehow really oddly
Eliminating the whole need for a reference here, oddly
content.explanation: A narrower focused beam separates and locates reflectors better at the focal depth, improving lateral resolution and sizing accuracy there.
distractors: Focusing does not change the material velocity.
Focusing does not remove artifacts such as grating lobes.
A reference is still required for sizing and sensitivity.

content.stem: Axial (depth) resolution, the ability to separate reflectors at slightly different depths, improves with:
options: A shorter pulse (higher bandwidth)
Just a plain longer pulse here,
Just a plain wider beam here, oddly
Lower frequency only here, oddly
content.explanation: Shorter, broadband pulses separate closely spaced depths better. Lateral resolution is governed mainly by beam width, which focusing improves.
distractors: A longer pulse worsens depth separation.
Beam width affects lateral, not axial, resolution.
Lower frequency generally lengthens the wavelength and degrades resolution.

content.stem: An indication that appears at an unexpected angle and tracks with the steering rather than the geometry may be:
options: A grating-lobe artifact
A real planar crack here
A backwall echo here
The coupling loss here
content.explanation: Grating lobes from element pitch can place spurious indications off the main beam. Recognizing them prevents calling an artifact as a flaw.
distractors: A real crack stays fixed to the part geometry, not to the steering artifact pattern.
A backwall echo comes from the known far surface, not an off-angle artifact.
Coupling loss shows as dropout, not an extra angled indication.

content.stem: A consistent indication at the weld root or counterbore that matches the part geometry is most likely:
options: A geometric (non-relevant) reflector to be recognized as such
Just plain always a rejectable crack here, somehow really oddly
Just a plain grating lobe here, somehow really quite oddly
A plain dead element here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Geometric features such as the root, counterbore, or mismatch reflect sound predictably. The evaluator distinguishes these from flaws using position, shape, and the scan plan.
distractors: Geometry reflectors are not automatically rejectable flaws.
A geometry echo is tied to the part shape, not the steering artifact pattern.
A dead element degrades the beam; it does not create a geometry-matched echo.

content.stem: Extra indications that appear at predictable later sound paths can arise from:
options: Mode conversion and multiple skips
A higher pulse repetition frequency
A fresh couplant
A new encoder
content.explanation: Mode conversion and skip paths produce predictable secondary signals. The evaluator accounts for these so they are not mistaken for additional flaws.
distractors: Pulse repetition frequency sets firing rate, not extra mode-converted paths.
Couplant condition does not create mode-converted indications.
The encoder records position; it does not create extra indications.

content.stem: Without angle-corrected gain, the same reference reflector across an S-scan sweep tends to read:
options: Different amplitudes at different angles
Identical amplitude at every angle here
Just plain zero at all the angles here
Just plain saturated at all the angles here
content.explanation: Sensitivity varies with steering angle, so ACG is applied so an equal reflector reads consistently. Interpreting amplitudes without it can misjudge relative response.
distractors: Equal amplitude across angles is the goal after ACG, not the uncorrected case.
A reference reflector returns a measurable signal, not zero.
A correctly set reference is not saturated across the sweep.

content.stem: Reading a reflector's true depth and horizontal position from an S-scan requires the display to be:
options: Volume (true-depth) corrected with correct velocity and wedge data
Just plain run at the whole maximum gain here, somehow really oddly
Just set to a single fixed angle here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain free of any whole encoder here, somehow really quite
content.explanation: True position comes from a corrected display built on the right velocity, wedge delay, and angles. Errors in these inputs mislocate reflectors.
distractors: Maximum gain does not establish correct geometry.
A single fixed angle is not how an S-scan presents the swept data.
Encoded position requires an encoder, not its absence.

content.stem: In coarse-grained or austenitic material, scattering tends to:
options: Raise background noise and lower the signal-to-noise ratio
Increase the whole signal-to-noise ratio here, somehow oddly
Just plain remove the whole attenuation here, somehow oddly
Sharpen the whole beam here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Grain scattering produces noise and attenuation that can mask real signals, so probe choice (for example lower frequency or dual TRL) and interpretation account for it.
distractors: Scattering degrades, not improves, signal-to-noise.
Scattering adds to attenuation rather than removing it.
Scattering blurs and weakens the beam, not sharpens it.

content.stem: Reflectors very close to the scanning surface can be hard to size because of:
options: The near-surface dead zone and limited resolution there
Just plain excessive material velocity here, somehow oddly
Just too low a whole couplant level here, somehow oddly
An oversized encoder step here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: Near-surface resolution is limited by the initial pulse and wedge, creating a region where sizing is unreliable, which the scan plan and technique address.
distractors: Material velocity is a fixed property, not the cause of the dead zone.
Couplant level does not create the near-surface dead zone.
Encoder step affects scan sampling, not the near-surface dead zone.

content.stem: A rough or branched crack can scatter sound, so its response may be:
options: Lower and more variable than a smooth planar reflector of the same size
Always higher than any other reflector here, somehow really quite oddly
Exactly equal to a flat-bottom hole here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Independent of the orientation here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Rough or multifaceted flaws scatter energy, so amplitude can be lower and erratic compared with a smooth specular reflector, which is why amplitude alone is unreliable for sizing.
distractors: Scattering can lower the response, so it is not always highest.
A real crack does not match a machined hole's response exactly.
Crack response still varies with orientation.

content.stem: If the material velocity is set too high, a reflector's computed depth will be:
options: Deeper than its true depth
Shallower than its true depth
Exactly correct
Unaffected
content.explanation: Depth is computed from time and velocity, so an overstated velocity converts the same travel time into a greater depth, mislocating the reflector. The evaluator verifies velocity before relying on positions.
distractors: Too high a velocity overstates, rather than understates, depth.
A wrong velocity does not give the correct depth.
Depth does depend on the velocity setting.

content.stem: Choosing the focal depth near the region of interest is done so that:
options: Reflectors there are resolved and sized most reliably
The whole thickness is always in perfect focus here
Just plain the couplant lasts longer here, somehow oddly
The encoder reads faster here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: A beam focused near the region of interest gives the best resolution there. A single focus cannot keep the whole thickness equally sharp, so focus is placed where sizing matters.
distractors: One focal setting cannot keep the entire thickness equally focused.
Focal depth is unrelated to couplant life.
Focal depth does not change the encoder rate.

content.stem: Loss of the expected backwall signal under a region can indicate:
options: A reflector or attenuator intercepting the beam, worth investigating
Just a perfectly clean part, always here, somehow really quite oddly
Just a plain higher frequency here, somehow really quite oddly enough
A plain new whole wedge here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
content.explanation: A backwall drop can mean a flaw or strong attenuator is blocking the path, so the evaluator investigates rather than assuming the area is sound.
distractors: A backwall loss is a reason to investigate, not proof of soundness.
Backwall behavior is not a frequency change.
Backwall loss is not caused by changing the wedge.

content.stem: Sweeping a range of angles in an S-scan helps the evaluator because flaws on a weld bevel:
options: Are favorably oriented to different angles at different depths
All respond best to one fixed angle here, somehow really oddly
Just plain never reflect the sound here, somehow really quite
Just only appear on the surface here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: The bevel and fusion faces present at varying orientations through the thickness, so different angles favor different flaws and depths, improving detection and characterization.
distractors: A single fixed angle does not favor all flaw orientations.
Fusion-face flaws do reflect sound when struck favorably.
Weld flaws are volumetric, not only on the surface.

content.stem: Selecting a higher frequency for an evaluation generally improves resolution but:
options: Reduces penetration and can raise grain noise
Just plain increases the penetration here, oddly
Eliminates the whole beam spread here, oddly
Removes the need to calibrate here, oddly
content.explanation: Higher frequency sharpens resolution yet attenuates faster and can raise noise in coarse material, a trade-off the evaluator weighs for the application.
distractors: Higher frequency reduces, not increases, penetration.
Beam spread still occurs at higher frequency.
Calibration is always required.

content.stem: Weak signals returning from the tips of a planar flaw are significant because they:
options: Support through-wall height sizing by diffraction
Indicate the whole couplant has failed here, oddly
Are always larger than the whole corner echo here
Mean the whole flaw is non-relevant here, oddly
content.explanation: Diffracted tip signals let the evaluator measure through-wall height more accurately than amplitude methods, especially for tall planar flaws. They are usually weaker than specular corner echoes.
distractors: Tip signals are a sizing aid, not a sign of coupling failure.
Tip diffraction signals are typically weaker than the corner reflection.
Tip signals help size the flaw; they do not make it non-relevant.

content.stem: When an unexpected indication appears, the evaluator first:
options: Determines whether it is a real reflector or an artifact or geometry
Just records it as a rejectable defect here, somehow really quite
Just plain deletes it from the data here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain totally ignores it here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Characterization starts by separating real flaws from artifacts and geometry using position, behavior, and the scan plan, before any sizing or acceptance decision.
distractors: Calling it a defect skips the characterization step.
Data is preserved, not deleted.
Indications are investigated, not ignored.

content.stem: If the probe is skewed relative to the scan axis, recorded reflector positions will be:
options: Shifted from their true location
Just plain more accurate here,
Just plain totally unchanged here
Plain set totally to zero here
content.explanation: Skew misaligns the beam and the encoded geometry, displacing indications. The evaluator looks for this when positions seem inconsistent and has the scan repeated if needed.
distractors: Skew degrades, not improves, positional accuracy.
Skew does change the recorded positions.
Skew shifts positions; it does not zero them.

content.stem: A steered angle near the array's steering limit should be interpreted carefully because:
options: Sensitivity and beam quality fall there
Sensitivity is highest there here, oddly
Just plain it needs no calibration here
It removes the whole grating lobes now
content.explanation: At extreme steering, response drops and artifacts grow, so amplitudes there are less reliable and the evaluator weighs that in interpretation.
distractors: Sensitivity falls, not peaks, near the steering limit.
Calibration still applies at all angles.
Extreme steering can worsen, not remove, grating lobes.

content.stem: A strong response where a planar flaw meets a surface (a corner) is produced by:
options: A corner-reflector (right-angle) return to the probe
Diffraction from the whole flaw tip here, somehow
Just plain grain scattering here, somehow really oddly
Couplant on the whole surface here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: A flaw breaking a surface forms a corner trap that returns a strong specular echo, useful for detection but separate from the weaker tip-diffraction signal used for height.
distractors: Tip diffraction gives a weaker signal from the flaw end, not the strong corner return.
Grain scattering produces noise, not the corner return.
Surface couplant does not produce the corner echo.

content.stem: Cross-checking an indication across the A-scan, S-scan, and top and side views helps the evaluator:
options: Confirm its position, extent, and nature
Increase the material velocity
Eliminate the need for a reference reflector
Bypass the procedure
content.explanation: Linked views give complementary information, so comparing them confirms whether an indication is real and where and how large it is.
distractors: Comparing views does not change material velocity.
A reference is still required; comparing views does not replace calibration.
The procedure is still followed.

content.stem: Deeper reflectors of equal size tend to give lower amplitudes before correction because of:
options: Attenuation and beam spread with distance
Higher frequency at the depth here, oddly
Lower material density at depth here, oddly
A plain shorter sound path here, oddly
content.explanation: Sound weakens with distance from attenuation and divergence, so depth-gain correction (TCG) is applied so equal reflectors read consistently for fair comparison.
distractors: Frequency does not increase with depth.
Material density does not drop with depth in a uniform part.
Deeper reflectors have a longer, not shorter, sound path.

content.stem: Trying to place the focal point beyond the aperture's near field will:
options: Not achieve true focusing there
Sharply focus the whole beam here
Increase material velocity here
Just eliminate the beam spread
content.explanation: Focusing is only effective within the near field, so a focal point set beyond it does not focus, and sizing in that region relies on the unfocused beam's wider spread.
distractors: Focusing cannot be achieved beyond the near field.
Focal settings do not change material velocity.
Beyond the near field the beam diverges; spread is not eliminated.

content.stem: Compared with a planar flaw, a volumetric flaw such as a cluster of porosity tends to:
options: Scatter sound in many directions, often giving rounded, lower or multiple signals
Give one strong specular echo only at normal incidence here, somehow really oddly
Just plain produce no response at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Always exceed a crack's amplitude here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Volumetric flaws scatter from many small surfaces, giving rounded or multiple responses that differ from a planar flaw's specular behavior, which aids characterization.
distractors: A single strong specular echo at normal incidence is more typical of a planar reflector.
Porosity does reflect sound and is detectable.
Volumetric responses are not always higher than a crack's.

content.stem: A worn wedge can mislead interpretation because it changes the:
options: Actual refracted angles and exit point
Material density of the whole part here
Just plain the acceptance criteria here
The number of the array elements here
content.explanation: Wedge wear shifts the real angles and beam exit, so positions and angle-based reasoning drift from the setup, which the evaluator verifies and corrects.
distractors: Wedge wear does not change the part's density.
Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the wedge.
Wedge wear does not change the element count.

content.stem: On an uncorrected angle-beam display, the horizontal scale is usually:
options: Sound path, which must be projected to get true depth
Just plain already the whole true depth here, somehow
Just the couplant thickness here, somehow really oddly
Just plain the whole scan length here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: An uncorrected angle display reads sound path, so depth and surface distance are derived by projection using the refracted angle. A corrected view does this automatically.
distractors: Sound path is not the same as true depth on an uncorrected display.
The scale is sound path, not couplant thickness.
The angle-beam display scale is sound path, not scan length.

content.stem: Classifying an indication as relevant or non-relevant is based on:
options: Its source and behavior judged against the geometry and procedure
Just plain its whole amplitude alone here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain the whole scan speed used here, somehow really quite
Just plain the whole cable used here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Relevance is decided by whether the indication comes from a flaw versus geometry or an artifact, using position, response, and the procedure, not display color.
distractors: Amplitude alone does not establish relevance; a strong echo can be geometry.
Scan speed does not determine whether an indication is relevant.
The cable used does not determine relevance.

content.stem: Before trusting reflector positions in the imaging, the evaluator confirms the focal-law setup was:
options: Verified on a reference block for angles and depth
Run at the whole fastest scan speed here, oddly
Built with the most focal laws possible here, oddly
Built with the largest possible aperture here, oddly
content.explanation: Position accuracy depends on a verified setup, so the evaluator checks that angles, depth, and sensitivity were confirmed on a reference before interpreting positions.
distractors: Scan speed does not validate the geometry.
More focal laws do not by themselves ensure correct positions.
A larger aperture alone does not verify the setup's angles or depth.

content.stem: An indication saturating at full screen height is a problem for sizing because:
options: Its true amplitude and extent cannot be measured while clipped
It proves the whole flaw is rejectable here, somehow really
Just plain it improves the resolution here, somehow really quite
It corrects the whole calibration here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: A clipped signal hides amplitude information, so gain is reduced to bring it on scale before amplitude-based sizing or comparison.
distractors: Saturation does not by itself establish rejection.
Saturation does not improve resolution.
Saturation does not correct calibration.

content.stem: Confirming a suspected planar flaw with more than one angle is useful because:
options: A favorable angle raises the response and helps confirm orientation
Just plain angles never change the response here, somehow really
Just it removes the whole need for sizing here, somehow really oddly
Just plain it totally guarantees the acceptance here, somehow really
content.explanation: Different angles intercept a planar flaw differently, so the angle that maximizes the response helps confirm the flaw and its orientation before sizing.
distractors: Response does change with angle for a planar flaw.
Confirming with angles does not replace sizing.
It aids characterization, not a guaranteed acceptance.

content.stem: Which statement reflects sound interpretation practice?
options: Amplitude is not a direct measure of flaw size; orientation, type, geometry, and artifacts must all be weighed
The strongest echo is always the largest flaw here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now
Every indication is a rejectable defect here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now today
Display color shows the flaw severity here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now today and then
content.explanation: The evaluator treats amplitude as one clue among several, separating real flaws from geometry and artifacts and using defined techniques to size and evaluate.
distractors: Amplitude depends on more than size, so the strongest echo is not always the largest flaw.
Many indications are geometry or artifacts, not defects.
Color encodes amplitude, not severity.

content.stem: The primary purpose of a scan plan is to define how the inspection will:
options: Cover the required examination volume with adequate sensitivity
Just plain use the whole least couplant here, somehow really
Just produce the smallest files here, somehow really quite oddly
Finish in the shortest time here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: A scan plan specifies angles, focal laws, offsets, and probe positions so the required volume is covered at the required sensitivity, per the code and procedure.
distractors: Minimizing couplant is not the purpose of the scan plan.
File size is not what the scan plan is designed around.
Speed is secondary to achieving the required coverage.

content.stem: Angles for a bevel weld are chosen so the beam strikes the fusion faces:
options: Near perpendicular to detect sidewall lack of fusion
At a grazing angle to skim past them here, oddly
Just only parallel to the whole surface here, oddly
Only straight down at the whole zero degrees here, oddly
content.explanation: Sidewall lack of fusion lies along the bevel, so angles are selected to hit those faces near normal incidence where the planar response is strongest.
distractors: A grazing angle reflects energy away and under-responds the flaw.
A surface-parallel beam barely intercepts the fusion face.
A single zero-degree beam does not address angled fusion faces.

content.stem: Beam simulation or ray tracing during scan-plan design is used to:
options: Confirm the chosen angles and offsets actually cover the weld volume
Just plain totally replace the calibration here, somehow really quite
Just set the whole acceptance criteria here, somehow really quite
Generate the whole inspection report here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Ray tracing shows where the beams go for given angles, focal laws, and offsets, so the designer verifies coverage of the root, fusion faces, and cap before scanning.
distractors: Simulation does not replace physical calibration.
Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the simulation.
The report is produced from acquired data, not the plan simulation.

content.stem: Covering the upper and lower parts of a weld from one side typically requires:
options: Both the first leg and the skip (second) leg
Just plain only the whole first leg here, oddly
Just plain no probe movement here, oddly
A whole zero-degree beam only here, oddly
content.explanation: The direct (first) leg and the reflected skip leg reach different depths, so coverage of root to cap from one offset uses both legs, with the probe moved through the offset range.
distractors: The first leg alone may not reach the full thickness.
Coverage requires moving the probe through the offset range.
A zero-degree beam does not cover angled fusion faces.

content.stem: Scanning a weld from both sides is planned because:
options: Some flaw orientations are only well detected from one side
Just one side is always sufficient here, somehow really oddly
It halves the couplant use here, somehow really quite oddly
It shortens the data files here, somehow really oddly now
content.explanation: Flaws angled toward one side respond poorly from the other, so two-sided coverage is planned where access allows to catch various orientations.
distractors: A single side can miss flaws favorable to the other side.
Two-sided scanning is for coverage, not couplant savings.
Two sides increase, not shorten, the data.

content.stem: The range of index offsets in the plan is set so that:
options: The beams sweep through the weld volume as the probe moves
The probe always sits on the whole weld cap here, oddly
Just plain the cable stays straight here, somehow really
Just the couplant stays cool here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Moving the probe through a planned offset range walks the beams across the weld cross-section, which combined with the angles covers the volume.
distractors: The probe is offset to angle into the weld, not parked on the cap.
Cable routing is not what sets the offset range.
Couplant temperature does not set the offset range.

content.stem: The skip distance for a given angle depends on the:
options: Material thickness and the refracted angle
The pulse repetition frequency here, oddly
The number of array elements here, oddly
The operator certification level here, oddly
content.explanation: Skip distance is a function of thickness and refracted angle, so the designer uses it to place offsets and predict where each leg covers.
distractors: Firing rate does not set the skip distance, which is geometric.
Element count does not set the skip distance.
Certification level does not change the geometry of the skip.

content.stem: When a raster or multiple passes are planned, adjacent passes are set to:
options: Overlap so no volume is left unexamined
Just plain leave the gaps to save time here
Just plain totally never touch here now
Just plain be spaced at random here
content.explanation: Overlap between passes prevents unexamined strips, ensuring the planned volume is fully covered.
distractors: Gaps would leave volume unexamined.
Passes must cover the area, not avoid touching.
Spacing follows the plan, not random choice.

content.stem: An S-scan is often chosen over an E-scan for weld bevels because it:
options: Insonifies the bevel with a range of angles from each position
Just plain uses only one whole fixed angle here, somehow oddly
Needs no whole focal laws here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just removes the whole need for offsets here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: The angular sweep of an S-scan addresses the varying bevel and flaw orientations from each position, while an E-scan holds one angle and steps the aperture.
distractors: A single fixed angle is the E-scan behavior, not the S-scan advantage.
Focal laws are still required for an S-scan.
Probe offsets are still part of the plan.

content.stem: After designing the plan, coverage is verified by checking that:
options: The root, fusion faces, and cap are all insonified
Just plain the scan finishes quickly here, oddly
Only the whole easiest zone is covered here, oddly
Just plain the fewest angles are used here, somehow
content.explanation: The designer confirms the beams reach every required zone, including the root and fusion faces, before the plan is used.
distractors: Speed is not the coverage check.
All required zones, not only the easy one, must be covered.
Adequate coverage, not the fewest angles, governs the design.

content.stem: For small-diameter pipe, the scan plan specifies a wedge that is:
options: Contoured to the pipe so coupling and angles stay correct
Just plain the whole flattest available here, somehow oddly
Just oversized for the bore here, somehow really oddly
Run without the whole couplant here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: A contoured wedge maintains contact and the intended refracted angles around the curvature, which a flat wedge would not on small diameters.
distractors: A flat wedge rocks on a curved surface, changing coupling and angles.
An oversized wedge does not ensure correct fit.
Coupling still requires couplant.

content.stem: When access prevents scanning from one side, the plan should:
options: Use alternative angles or additional positions and record the limitation
Claim the full coverage anyway here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just plain skip that whole volume silently here, somehow really quite
Lower the acceptance criteria here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
content.explanation: Where access limits coverage, the designer adapts angles and positions to cover as much as possible and documents what could not be examined, rather than overstating coverage.
distractors: Claiming coverage that was not achieved is false.
Uncovered volume is documented, not omitted silently.
Acceptance criteria are not lowered to mask coverage gaps.

content.stem: Reliable root coverage in a single-sided weld often depends on:
options: The correct leg and angle reaching the root region
Just plain the whole maximum gain alone here, oddly
A higher pulse repetition frequency here, oddly
A whole longer scan here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: The root sits at a specific depth and position, so the plan selects the leg and angle that place a favorable beam there, verified by simulation.
distractors: Gain alone does not place the beam at the root.
Firing rate does not place the beam at the root.
Scan length alone does not ensure the beam reaches the root.

content.stem: If the weld cap blocks the needed probe offset, the plan may call to:
options: Dress the cap so the probe can reach the offset
Just scan only the whole cap surface here, oddly
Just plain abandon the inspection here, oddly
Use a whole zero-degree beam only here, oddly
content.explanation: Where coverage requires it, the cap is dressed flush so the probe can sit at the planned offset, per the procedure.
distractors: Scanning only the cap surface does not cover the weld volume.
Access issues are addressed, not a reason to abandon the job.
A zero-degree beam alone does not cover the angled volume.

content.stem: Using multiple focal-law groups in a plan can:
options: Cover several angle ranges or zones in one pass
Remove the need for calibration here, oddly
Just plain eliminate the whole encoder here, oddly
Just plain totally avoid the procedure here
content.explanation: Several groups can acquire complementary coverage together, configured in the setup and still calibrated and position-encoded.
distractors: Multiple groups still require calibration.
Position encoding is still needed.
The procedure is still followed.

content.stem: For thickness or corrosion mapping rather than weld flaw detection, the plan typically uses:
options: Zero-degree (straight-beam) coverage over the area
Just plain only the high steered angles here, oddly
Just plain totally no whole encoding here, oddly
Just plain a single whole A-scan point here, oddly
content.explanation: Wall-thickness and corrosion mapping use straight-beam coverage to measure remaining wall across the area, a different goal from angled weld inspection.
distractors: High steered angles are for weld bevels, not flat thickness mapping.
Mapping is encoded so the data ties to position.
A single point does not map an area.

content.stem: A good plan also ensures that across the examined volume the:
options: Sensitivity stays adequate (via TCG/ACG) at all required depths and angles
Gain is fixed with no correction here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Beam is left unfocused at all depths here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain the whole cable is the shortest here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Coverage is only meaningful if sensitivity is adequate throughout, so depth and angle gain corrections are part of designing a usable plan.
distractors: Uncorrected fixed gain leaves deep or steered reflectors under-responded.
An unfocused beam does not ensure adequate sensitivity across the volume.
Cable length does not set sensitivity.

content.stem: Complex geometry such as a nozzle or branch connection complicates the plan because:
options: Curvature and varying thickness change the beam paths and coverage
Just it removes the whole need for angles here, somehow really oddly
It makes the whole calibration unnecessary here, somehow really
Just it eliminates the whole artifacts here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: Changing curvature and thickness alter where beams go, so coverage must be worked out for the specific geometry, often with simulation and extra positions.
distractors: Angles are still required, often more of them.
Calibration is still required.
Complex geometry can add, not remove, geometric indications.

content.stem: Where possible, inspecting a zone on the first leg is often preferred because:
options: The beam has spread and attenuated less, giving cleaner response
The skip leg is always blocked here, somehow really quite oddly
Just plain it needs no whole calibration here, somehow really oddly
Just it totally avoids the encoder here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: First-leg paths are shorter with less spread and attenuation, so response is generally cleaner, though skip legs are used where geometry requires.
distractors: The skip leg is used routinely, not always blocked.
Calibration still applies on the first leg.
The encoder is still used.

content.explanation: Authorizing the report is an accountable act affirming the work and conclusions are the evaluator's responsibility within their scope.
distractors: It signifies responsibility, not mere observation.
It does not transfer responsibility to the client.
It affirms the evaluation was performed.

content.stem: Which statement about procedures and responsibilities is correct?
options: Work to a qualified procedure within your scope, apply the governing code and edition, report findings honestly, and refer decisions beyond your qualification
Use just any procedure and invent the criteria as needed here and now today really indeed now truly so really now today so really now today so really now today so really now today so
Pass the work under pressure whenever asked here and now today really indeed now truly so really now today so really now today so really now today so really now today so really now today so
Falsify the records just to keep the schedule here and now today really indeed now truly so really now today so really now today so really now today so really now today so really now today so
content.explanation: Sound practice follows a qualified procedure within scope, applies the correct governing criteria, reports truthfully, and escalates decisions that exceed the evaluator's qualification.
distractors: Procedures and criteria are governed, not improvised.
Work is not passed under pressure.
Records are never falsified.

content.stem: Automated ultrasonic testing of girth welds is permitted under API 1104 when it is:
options: Run faster than radiography across the spread as a rule
Preferred by the AUT operator over manual UT
Qualified to the standard's procedure and system rules
Cheaper to deploy than a manual UT crew
distractors: Speed does not authorize a method.
Operator preference does not qualify a system.
Cost is not a qualification basis.
content.explanation: AUT is allowed when the procedure and system are qualified per the standard, typically proven on test welds with known flaws.

content.stem: Zonal discrimination divides the weld for AUT into:
options: Horizontal slices taken along the length of the pipe as a rule
Two equal halves split at the weld centerline
Random sampling windows placed around the weld
Vertical zones across the wall, each with its own focal laws
distractors: AUT zones are through-wall, not lengthwise slices.
It is not a simple two-part split.
Coverage is systematic, not random.
content.explanation: The weld bevel is split into through-wall zones; each zone is covered by dedicated focal laws and channels.

content.stem: An AUT zonal system is calibrated on a reference standard containing:
options: A single side-drilled hole placed at mid-wall only
Targets that represent each zone of the weld bevel
No reflectors at all, set by a free-run scan
The production weld itself used as the standard
distractors: One mid-wall hole cannot set every zone.
Calibration needs known reflectors.
The production weld is not the calibration standard.
content.explanation: The calibration block carries targets (such as notches or flat-bottom holes) positioned to set sensitivity for each zone.

content.stem: Dedicated coupling-check channels are included in an AUT setup to:
options: Flag loss of acoustic coupling during the scan
Measure the pipe wall temperature during the run
Record the welder's identity for the data log
Time the scanner's travel speed around the pipe
distractors: Coupling channels watch sound transfer, not temperature.
They do not log personnel.
They are not a timing device.
content.explanation: Coupling monitor channels detect coupling loss so data gaps are caught and re-scanned.

content.stem: TOFD is often paired with zonal AUT mainly to:
options: Remove the need for any system calibration at all itself
Take the place of the operator running the scan
Improve detection and height sizing of mid-wall flaws
Speed up the pipe coating after the weld passes
distractors: TOFD still requires calibration.
It does not remove the operator.
It is unrelated to coating.
content.explanation: TOFD complements zonal pulse-echo by improving mid-wall detection and through-wall height measurement for sizing.

content.stem: When AUT results are judged by the alternative acceptance criteria, the governing inputs include:
options: Flaw height and length assessed against an ECA
The film density measured through the weld
The penetrameter hole count seen on the shot
The radiographic technique chart for the joint
distractors: Density is a radiographic term.
Penetrameters belong to radiography.
RT technique charts do not apply to AUT/ECA.
content.explanation: Alternative (ECA) acceptance evaluates flaw height and length against limits derived from stress and fitness-for-service analysis.

content.stem: If AUT is instead judged by workmanship criteria, indications are limited mainly by their:
options: Its color as shown on the analyst's display
Its length within the relevant weld zone
Its distance from the start point of the scan
The number of channels firing during the scan
distractors: Color is not an acceptance parameter.
Position along the weld is not the limit.
Channel count is a setup detail.
content.explanation: Under the workmanship route, indication length governs, applied per zone, similar in spirit to the radiographic length limits.

content.stem: Through-wall height of a flaw matters under API 1104 AUT primarily when:
options: The pipe is under six inches in diameter
Radiography was also performed on the joint as well
The operator running the scan holds Level I
Alternative (ECA) acceptance criteria are in force
distractors: Diameter does not switch on height sizing.
RT does not trigger AUT height rules.
Level does not set the acceptance route.
content.explanation: Height (through-wall extent) is a key input for ECA-based acceptance; workmanship criteria lean on length.

content.stem: An AUT system is typically proven by scanning:
options: A blank pipe with no flaws machined into it itself
A radiograph taken of a similar girth weld
The calibration certificate read on its own
Qualification welds with known, measured flaws
distractors: A flaw-free coupon cannot prove detection.
A radiograph does not qualify a UT system.
A certificate is not a detection trial.
content.explanation: System performance is demonstrated on welds with intentional, characterized flaws to show detection and sizing capability.

content.stem: The AUT data display for a girth weld is commonly read as a:
options: A strip/mapping view of channels around the weld
A single A-scan trace viewed on its own
A processed photographic film of the joint itself
A numeric table carrying no imaging at all
distractors: A single A-scan does not map the full weld.
AUT produces electronic data, not film.
Imaging, not just numbers, is used.
content.explanation: Zonal AUT is interpreted from a strip-chart/mapping display showing each channel around the weld.

content.stem: Position accuracy along the weld in AUT depends on the:
options: The film identification letters on the shot
The brand of couplant used during the scan
The ambient light level at the work site
An encoder tracking the scanner's travel
distractors: Film letters are radiographic.
Couplant brand does not set position.
Light does not locate indications.
content.explanation: An encoder ties each data point to a circumferential position so indications can be located and re-examined.

content.stem: A planar crack-like flaw detected by AUT is:
options: Ignored entirely whenever it measures short
Acceptable as long as it sits away from the root itself
The most critical type, tight under ECA height limits
Outside what AUT is actually able to detect
distractors: Short planar flaws still matter under ECA.
Location does not make a crack acceptable.
AUT is well suited to planar flaws.
content.explanation: Planar, crack-like flaws are the most severe and are tightly limited, particularly by height under ECA.

content.stem: AUT calibration validity can be affected by a change in:
options: Part or wedge temperature between cal and scan
The welder's helmet shade used on the joint itself
The color of paint applied to the pipe
The data file name chosen for the scan
distractors: Helmet shade is unrelated to UT.
Paint color does not shift velocity.
File naming does not affect sound.
content.explanation: Temperature shifts velocity and wedge behavior, so significant change can invalidate the calibration.

content.stem: An AUT zonal scan is arranged so that the combined zones provide:
options: Through-wall coverage of the weld and fusion faces
Coverage of the finished weld cap only
Coverage of the root bead region only
A single-pass surface check of the weld on the joint
distractors: Cap-only coverage misses the volume.
Root-only coverage misses the rest.
AUT is volumetric, not a surface check.
content.explanation: Zones are set so the full weld bevel and fusion faces are covered through the wall.

content.stem: Final accept/reject of an AUT-examined weld rests with the:
options: The AUT operator running the scan, on their own
The company, applying the chosen acceptance criteria
The scanner manufacturer that built the rig
The software vendor that supplied the analysis tool itself
distractors: The operator reports; disposition is the company's.
Equipment makers do not disposition welds.
Software does not decide acceptance.
content.explanation: The company dispositions the weld using the criteria in force, informed by the AUT data.

content.stem: A weld section rejected by AUT and then repaired is:
options: Accepted on the strength of the repair record alone itself
Re-examined to the same method and acceptance criteria
Judged the second time by clearly relaxed limits
Exempt from any further AUT once the repair is done
distractors: A record is not re-inspection.
Limits do not relax for repairs.
Repairs require re-examination.
content.explanation: The repair is re-inspected to the same method and acceptance basis as the original scan.

content.stem: AUT for API 1104 compliance is run by personnel who are:
options: Any available member of the spread crew
Qualified and certified for the AUT technique
Approved by the coating crew on the line
Chosen on seniority among the hands present itself
distractors: Untrained crew cannot run AUT.
Coating crews do not certify UT.
Seniority is not certification.
content.explanation: AUT is performed by qualified, certified personnel under the applicable qualification provisions.

content.stem: AUT results submitted for API 1104 acceptance should record:
options: Only a simple pass or fail stamp on the joint as a rule
The film density measured through the weld
Indication location, length, and height where required
The radiographic IQI placed beside the weld
distractors: A bare stamp is not a usable record.
Density is a radiographic field.
IQIs are radiographic, not AUT.
content.explanation: The AUT report captures each indication's position and size, with height where ECA applies.

content.stem: Compared with conventional manual UT, AUT zonal discrimination adds:
options: Lower sensitivity than manual UT by design
A requirement to also shoot a radiograph
Encoded, channel-per-zone coverage with recorded data
The removal of all calibration from the process itself
distractors: AUT is not designed to be less sensitive.
AUT does not require film.
AUT still requires calibration.
content.explanation: Zonal AUT provides systematic, encoded, recordable coverage zone by zone, unlike a manual sweep.
